Applied.Outcome: Resolved with no reply: the recommendation went in. Arguments( argv, { Flags, Positional, Rest } ) answers { Options, Positional, Rest }; Flags are { Name, Takes: value | number | flag, Key }; Rest for the Desktop and the Server, whose remaining arguments go to Start.js.

Replies.Text:
The shape of App.Arguments. The four parsers differ in one way that matters: the Sidecar and the Client parse every argument themselves and refuse what they do not know, while the Desktop and the Server take their own flag out (--connect, --open) and hand the rest (--config, --port, a folder) to src/Start.js, which parses them. So the shared parser needs a "rest" mode.

Recommendation: Arguments( argv, { Flags, Positional, Rest } ) answers { Options, Positional, Rest }. Flags is a list of { Name: "--port", Takes: "value" | "number" | "flag", Key: "Port" }; a flag that takes a value throws "--port needs a port number" when none follows or the next word starts with --; "number" also checks a whole positive number. Options holds each flag by its Key (Connect, Port, Config, Open, Headless, Scope), null or false when absent. Positional true allows one bare argument (the folder), answered as Positional, else a bare argument throws. Rest true keeps every argument the Flags do not name, in order, for Start.js; Rest false (the default) throws on an unknown argument. The Electron switches and the executable (and the app folder from the checkout) are taken out first, as all four do today. A folder is a value the app resolves itself, so there is no "folder" kind. Resolve with no reply to take it.

Anchor.Text: a test keeps the look lists equal

Applied.Outcome: Resolved with no reply: the recommendation went in. The two lists stay plain constants, and a test over theme.js's PALETTES and electron/Settings.js fails when they differ.

Replies.Text:
How the look lists are kept to one. Today the themes are written four times: theme.js PALETTES in the browser, and THEMES, DARK_THEMES and SCALES in the three Settings modules (the Desktop's even lists the dark ones twice). The Settings modules move to electron/Settings.js, so the count becomes two: the browser script and the Node module, which cannot require each other.

The ways: (a) a test reads theme.js, finds PALETTES and asserts electron/Settings.js lists the same ids with the same dark ones; (b) one JSON file (public/js/themes.json) both read, theme.js fetching it before it paints, which puts a request before the first paint and a flash of the default theme; (c) electron/Settings.js reads theme.js's text at load and picks PALETTES out with a regex, which is brittle. Recommendation: (a), the test, as the plan says: the two lists stay plain constants, and a palette added to one side without the other fails the suite. Resolve with no reply to take it.

Anchor.Text: electron/Servers.js is the Servers store's home

Applied.Outcome: Resolved with no reply: the recommendation went in. The Servers store lives in electron/Servers.js, with the applications' shared code.

Replies.Text:
Where the Servers store lives. It is the list of saved Servers an application connects to (Name, Url, the token kept by the OS), plain functions over a settings object, Electron-free; today in client/Settings.js, and after Step 5 the Desktop's too. It could live in src/ (Electron-free code) or in electron/ (what the applications share).

Recommendation: electron/Servers.js. src/ is the server's code, which has no notion of a saved Server to connect to; electron/ is already the applications' shared place and Page.js there is Electron-free too. The module is tested in plain node either way. Resolve with no reply to take it.
